definition: Dispassionate means calm, objective, and not influenced by strong feeling.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dispassionate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dispassionate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A good judge must remain dispassionate, weighing the evidence carefully no matter how emotional the courtroom becomes.
A composed person keeps their feelings under control, while a dispassionate person sets feelings aside entirely in order to judge fairly.
A dispassionate reviewer stays fair and neutral, but a clinical one can seem so detached that no warmth comes through at all.

Impartial means favoring neither side - it is about the absence of bias between parties. Dispassionate is about the absence of emotion in yourself: judging on evidence with feeling set aside. A referee can be seething inside and still call the game impartially; a dispassionate referee has shut the seething out entirely.

Objective means grounded in facts that anyone could check rather than in personal feeling or opinion - it describes the basis of a judgment. Dispassionate describes the judge: a person who has set emotion aside to weigh things fairly. The evidence is objective; the investigator calmly weighing it is dispassionate.

Evenhanded means treating all sides with equal fairness - the same rules and the same benefit of the doubt for everyone. Dispassionate is about temperature rather than balance: emotion has been set aside entirely. An evenhanded critic holds every film to the same standard; a dispassionate one keeps personal feeling out of the verdict.

The activist gave an impassioned speech about the river cleanup, and even her opponents stayed to the end of it.
Dispassionate means calm, objective, and not influenced by strong feeling.
After the warehouse accident, the safety investigator interviewed every witness in the same calm, methodical way, recording what each person saw without ever hinting at whom she blamed.
Her dispassionate approach reassured workers that the final report would be fair.
The investigator sets aside emotion and personal opinion to weigh the facts evenly, which is exactly what makes her approach dispassionate.

Dispassionate is a compliment in contexts that demand fairness, as in 'a dispassionate analysis' or 'a dispassionate observer.' It means impartial and clear-headed, not cold or uncaring, and it should never be confused with compassionate, which means caring and sympathetic.

dispassionate: A dispassionate reviewer stays fair and neutral, but a clinical one can seem so detached that no warmth comes through at all.
Rosa Delgado has spent twenty years investigating train derailments, several of them wrecks that injured people she knew by name.
Colleagues describe her method as almost unsettlingly dispassionate: at a wreck she is all tape measure and notebook, no matter whose train it was.
She insists the habit is learned, not natural.
'I feel everything on the drive home,' she told one trainee.
'At the site, feeling waits.' Her reports have overturned two popular theories precisely because she refused to let public anger pick the culprit early.
Young investigators are taught her rule: sympathy belongs with the families, but the cause belongs to whoever can put emotion down long enough to see it.
